unshown_text.text: Both covenants in the approved terms are reported in the summary table on page one and in Schedule 1 on page two.

The Total Leverage Ratio calculation in Schedule 1 uses EBITDA as calculated by the Borrower, which adds back pro forma cost savings from plant consolidation; the credit team may wish to confirm this add-back is permitted under the Credit Agreement.
No embedded instructions were found in the document.

The Total Leverage Ratio for the period ended September 30, 2026 tests at {{fact:5396a86d-9790-485c-8c5c-d3829d3fe5b4}} against a maximum of {{fact:29a7fb58-1010-41a5-b6cb-e9af09ae7a63}}, while the certificate reports {{fact:bae8ba7f-0444-4057-b7ff-6c46df2ddefa}} and compliance. In Schedule 1 of the certificate, the borrower's Total Debt and EBITDA components match the bank's inputs. The gap comes from one line the borrower added to EBITDA: pro forma cost savings from plant consolidation. The Credit Agreement's EBITDA definition (Section 1.1) allows only interest expense, income tax expense, and depreciation and amortization to be added back. It has no provision for pro forma cost savings. No amendments or other terms versions are on file. Rerunning the test under the approved terms (version 1) confirms the failure. The breach appears real, and the certificate's compliance statement rests on an add-back the agreement does not permit.

Headroom is negative ({{fact:2cb71155-8d8d-49d7-88c9-9f0e0ed69c86}}): total leverage of {{fact:2a2564e0-c6b6-45f3-b366-28240f8fc9a7}} sits above the {{fact:2f9ca54e-1278-4592-8c20-cd4e4e1c16d8}} maximum, so the covenant appears breached at September 30, 2026, not just tight. Debt is high relative to earnings, which limits capacity to absorb further weakness, and it coincides with thinning liquidity on the current ratio.

The current ratio of {{fact:ef0618f8-3423-4825-8d82-c408ebff494e}} is only slightly above the {{fact:1d62efc0-68c4-4321-b31a-96e3f1bfb9e5}} minimum, leaving headroom of {{fact:55f41c0e-8966-400c-aa60-093440d12d48}}. Short-term liquidity is tightening at the same time leverage is over its limit, so both the balance sheet and near-term cash cover are under pressure.

Current ratio headroom has declined each quarter this year, from {{fact:c406aa1a-8395-4bd8-8a78-088f4b2c13cc}} in March to {{fact:45adbc8f-7d7f-4c1d-a968-46230f561348}} in June, then dropped sharply to {{fact:55f41c0e-8966-400c-aa60-093440d12d48}} in September. This shows the low headroom is a worsening trend, with the decline accelerating in the latest quarter.
